newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech mkt could revive soon if govt acts-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech mkt could revive soon if govt acts-analysts.

text.p: The Czech capital market, hit hard by investor fears over a lack of transparency, would take only six months to revive if the government moves to tighten regulation and oversight, analysts said on Monday.

Speaking before a seminar on market regulation, Stephen Ross, Professor of Finance at Yale University and Director of Roll and Ross Asset Management said the appetite of emerging market investors was so great, the Czech market could return to favour quickly if tightening moves were made.

"There is no country in the world better poised for economic prosperity than (here)...(but) what is done with the capital markets here in the next year or two will determine how rapidly that prosperity will be achieved," he said.
"I believe that with the proper measures in place within six months you would see a very significant recovery in terms of international investments in the Czech Republic," he added.
Despite being eastern Europe's most-capitalised bourse, the Czech market has long been plagued by inadequate legislation that investors complain fails to provide protection for minority shareholders.
The problems have restrained the PSE which sees on average $4-$6 million of stock changing hands each day, compared with $15 million turnover in Warsaw, a much smaller market.

But a panel of analysts who will speak at the conference on Tuesday told journalists the government signalled its intention to tackle the issue last month when, as part of a package of measures to kick-start the economy, it said it would set up an inter-ministerial team to fight crime in the markets.
It also proposed a law to create a special body to fight crime in the banking sector, in particular, and promised an investigation into delays in prosecuting economic crime.

"The country's economic and capital market have converged in recent months, and this has helped push the issue," said Howard Goldman, head of the Foundation for the Development of the Czech Capital Market.
"The government now doesn't have the luxury to not act," he added.

The analysts said that in addition to the administrative measures already announced, forcing the country's closed-ended investment funds to open would help make them more accountable to shareholders and bring further transparency to the market.
They added that companies must also be forced to reveal more information to help bring back investor confidence.
"There is an opinion that regulation hinders the capital market, but in fact, it helps them work properly," said Joseph Stiglitz, Vice-president and Chief Economist at the World bank.
He said that this would in turn help the Czech economy, which has shown signs of recession in recent months.
Stiglitz said that countries with tight regulations and strong banking systems tend to have almost double the GDP growth than those without.

Real Czech GDP grew at 4.4 percent, year-on-year in 1996, slightly below expectations. Klaus said in releasing the economic reform package that if real GDP growth hit 2.7 percent this year -- only half of the original government estimate -- it would be " a success".
